chunks: If a man leaves behind a benefactor or one upon whom favor was bestowed, and leaves no heir other than him, then the estate belongs to him. If he leaves benefactors or those upon whom favor was bestowed, men and women, then the estate is divided among them, with the male receiving the share of two females.

If he leaves the sons and daughters of his benefactor or of the one upon whom favor was bestowed, and leaves no heir other than them, then the estate belongs to the sons and daughters of his mawlā, with the male receiving the share of two females, because al-walāʾ is a bond like the bond of lineage.

Whenever he leaves an heir from among blood relatives, whether the lineage is near or distant, and also leaves his benefactor or the one upon whom favor was bestowed, then the estate belongs to the heir from among the blood relatives, and the mawlā has no share.

Because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: “And those related by blood are nearer to one another in the Book of Allah than the believers and the Emigrants, except that you may do kindness to your allies.”
That means making a bequest for them of something, or the heirs giving them something from the inheritance as a gift.

key_terms.الْوَصِيَّةَ: a bequest made from the estate
key_terms.الْوَلَاءَ: the bond of clientage or affiliation that can establish inheritance rights
key_terms.لُحْمَةٌ كَلُحْمَةِ النَّسَبِ: a bond comparable to the bond of lineage
key_terms.مَوَالِيَ مُنْعِمِينَ: benefactor-mawālī connected through manumission or favor

ai.seo_question: When does a mawlā inherit, and do blood relatives take precedence over walāʾ in inheritance?
ai.summary: This hadith sets out the legal ruling of inheritance through walāʾ, giving the estate to the mawlā when there are no blood heirs, and distributing it among eligible male and female recipients according to the standard rule of the male receiving the share of two females. It also establishes that blood relatives take precedence over mawālī in inheritance, supported by the Qur'anic principle that kin are more entitled to one another, while kindness to allies may still be shown through a bequest or gift.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: If a man leaves behind a benefactor or a person upon whom he has bestowed favors and has no other heir, the wealth belongs to that individual. However, if he leaves behind multiple benefactors or those upon whom favors were bestowed, both men and women, the wealth is to be divided among them, with the male receiving the share equal to that of two females.

If he leaves behind the sons and daughters of his benefactor or the one upon whom he bestowed favors, and there is no other heir, the wealth belongs to the sons and daughters of his benefactor, with the male receiving the share equal to that of two females. This is because the bond of loyalty (wala') is like the bond of kinship.

However, if he leaves behind an heir from his blood relatives, whether closely or distantly related, along with his benefactor or the one upon whom he bestowed favors, the wealth belongs to the blood relative, and the benefactor receives nothing.

This is because Allah (swt), the Mighty and Majestic, says:
"Those who are related by blood are more entitled to inherit from each other in the Book of Allah (swt) than the believers and the emigrants, except that you do kindness to your allies,"
(Surah Al-Ahzab 33:6),
This meaning through a will for them or by the heirs gifting them something from the inheritance.
